stages.name: Family
stages.note: Book frames stages by order of magnitude of employees ('1s'). Everyone knows everyone; founders do everything. Some secondary summaries say 1-10; the order-of-magnitude framing (1-9) is the most consistent.

stages.name: Tribe
stages.note: '10s' of employees. First managers and departments appear; founder still knows everyone by name.

stages.name: Village
stages.note: '100s'. Formal structure, HR, layered management; founder no longer knows everyone. Chris Yeh: a village 'does in fact have formal structure'.

stages.name: City
stages.note: '1,000s'. Specialists, multiple business units; founder role shifts to resource allocation, strategy, alignment.

stages.name: Nation
stages.note: '10,000s'+. Multiple product lines/BUs; balance optimizing the core vs. incubating new lines. Revenue thresholds ($10M/$100M/$1B/$5B) appear in some secondary write-ups (e.g. David Cummings 2015) but are NOT part of the headcount definition.

stage_source: https://davidcummings.org/2015/12/13/the-startup-stages-in-blitzscaling/ (stage names + headcount order of magnitude: 1s/10s/100s/1,000s/10,000s, from Hoffman's Stanford Blitzscaling course); corroborated by https://www.antoinebuteau.com/blitzscaling-book-summary/ and https://blog.servicerocket.com/podcasts/ep.-93-chris-yeh-blitzscaling-is-about-going-from-zero-to-one-billion

artifacts.title: Blitzscaling defined
artifacts.quote: prioritising speed over efficiency in an environment of uncertainty
artifacts.speaker: Reid Hoffman (as quoted by GIC ThinkSpace, 2019)
artifacts.summary: Hoffman and Chris Yeh's 'Blitzscaling' (2018, from their Stanford course) defines blitzscaling as prioritizing speed over efficiency in the face of uncertainty. The phrase 'in the face of uncertainty' is the widely repeated book-summary wording; the verbatim string here is GIC's rendering of Hoffman's definition. The book text itself was not directly accessible.
artifacts.lesson: Speed is a weapon only when winner-take-most dynamics make being first-to-scale worth the waste.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Player first chooses a 'Blitz' growth posture (spend > revenue to accelerate headcount/compute).

artifacts.title: Embrace chaos
artifacts.speaker: Reid Hoffman & Chris Yeh
artifacts.summary: First of the book's 'nine counterintuitive rules of blitzscaling'. Hoffman: blitzscaling requires discipline to honour a fundamental, counter-intuitive rule - embrace chaos - at every stage, expecting customer complaints, 'embarrassing' products and management crash-and-burns as by-products. Commonly cited full list (secondary summaries, wording varies): Embrace Chaos; Hire Right Now, Not the Right Person; Tolerate 'Bad' Management; Launch a Product That Embarrasses You; Let Fires Burn; Do Things That Don't Scale; Ignore Your Customers; Raise Too Much Money; Evolve Your Culture.
artifacts.lesson: At hypergrowth, order is a luxury; the cost is real and accrues as org debt.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Org chaos meter exceeds threshold while growth is still positive.

artifacts.title: Let fires burn
artifacts.speaker: Reid Hoffman & Chris Yeh
artifacts.summary: One of the nine counterintuitive rules: you cannot fight every fire while blitzscaling, so focus on the big fires that could destroy the company and let smaller ones burn. Paired rules 'Tolerate bad management' and 'Ignore your customers' (i.e., customer complaints, when growth outpaces service) are also in the book's list per multiple summaries.
artifacts.lesson: Triage is strategy; but a fire you ignore can become the one that kills you.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: 3+ unresolved incident events open simultaneously (safety, PR, infra) while player keeps shipping.

artifacts.title: Launched too late
artifacts.quote: If you're not embarrassed by the first version of your product, you've launched too late.
artifacts.speaker: Reid Hoffman
artifacts.summary: Hoffman's long-standing aphorism (Eric Ries recalls him saying it years earlier at LinkedIn); earliest dated written instance found is his tweet of 2017-03-29, introduced with 'You may have heard me say:', and his companion essay 'If There Aren't Any Typos In This Essay, We Launched Too Late!'. Wording varies slightly across retellings ('If you are not...'). Became the book's 'Launch a product that embarrasses you' rule.
artifacts.lesson: Shipping teaches faster than polishing; perfectionism is a speed tax.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Player ships a model/product with low eval polish and it still gains users.

artifacts.title: Assembling the airplane on the way down
artifacts.quote: Starting a company is jumping off a cliff and assembling the airplane on the way down.
artifacts.speaker: Reid Hoffman (CNBC 'The Brave Ones')
artifacts.summary: Hoffman's version is attested from at least 2016 (variant: 'throwing yourself off the cliff and assembling an airplane on the way down'); the 2018 CNBC wording is verbatim. Hoffman did not originate the image: Quote Investigator traces 'jump off the cliff and ... make wings on the way down' to Ray Bradbury (1986, with a precursor in 1979).
artifacts.lesson: Founding is committing before you're ready; the airplane must be built faster than gravity.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Game start / founding the lab with runway under 12 months.

artifacts.title: Startup = Growth
artifacts.quote: A startup is a company designed to grow fast.
artifacts.speaker: Paul Graham
artifacts.summary: Opening line of Graham's September 2012 essay. Same essay: 'A good growth rate during YC is 5-7% a week. If you can hit 10% a week you're doing exceptionally well.'
artifacts.lesson: Growth is the defining metric; everything else is downstream.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Weekly user/revenue growth >= 5% for 4 consecutive weeks (10% unlocks 'exceptional' flavor).

artifacts.title: Make something people want
artifacts.quote: About a month after we started Y Combinator we came up with the phrase that became our motto: Make something people want.
artifacts.speaker: Paul Graham ('Be Good')
artifacts.summary: YC's motto, coined about a month after YC started in 2005 and printed on YC T-shirts. Graham traces it to Viaweb's early pivot away from building something customers didn't want.
artifacts.lesson: Demand, not technology, is the scarce input.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: First product reaches organic (non-paid) adoption above threshold.

artifacts.title: Three things
artifacts.quote: You need three things to create a successful startup: to start with good people, to make something customers actually want, and to spend as little money as possible.
artifacts.speaker: Paul Graham ('How to Start a Startup', Harvard talk/essay)
artifacts.summary: March 2005 essay from the talk that preceded YC's founding the same month. Note the frugality clause sits in tension with blitzscaling.
artifacts.lesson: Frugality and blitzscaling are opposite bets; know which one you are making.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Player reaches first milestone with burn below a frugality threshold.

artifacts.title: Do things that don't scale
artifacts.quote: One of the most common types of advice we give at Y Combinator is to do things that don't scale.
artifacts.speaker: Paul Graham
artifacts.summary: July 2013 essay. Examples: Airbnb founders going door to door in New York recruiting hosts and improving listings; Stripe's 'Collison installation' ('At YC we use the term "Collison installation" for the technique they invented') - setting users up on the spot rather than sending a link. Also one of Blitzscaling's nine rules.
artifacts.lesson: Manual hustle bootstraps the flywheel; automate only once you know what works.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Player assigns founders/researchers to hand-onboard enterprise customers.

artifacts.title: Ramen profitable
artifacts.quote: Ramen profitable means a startup makes just enough to pay the founders' living expenses.
artifacts.speaker: Paul Graham
artifacts.summary: July 2009 essay: reaching ramen profitability changes a startup's relationship with investors because it can no longer be starved.
artifacts.lesson: Survival optionality is leverage in fundraising.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Revenue first covers base (non-compute) payroll.

artifacts.title: Default alive or default dead?
artifacts.quote: Half the founders I talk to don't know whether they're default alive or default dead.
artifacts.speaker: Paul Graham
artifacts.summary: October 2015 essay. The test: assuming expenses stay constant and revenue growth continues at its recent rate, do you reach profitability on the money you have left? Trevor Blackwell built a calculator for it.
artifacts.lesson: Know whether your current trajectory survives without the next round.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Projected runway (constant burn, trailing growth) hits zero before break-even: show 'DEFAULT DEAD' banner.

artifacts.title: Founder mode
artifacts.quote: In effect there are two different ways to run a company: founder mode and manager mode.
artifacts.speaker: Paul Graham
artifacts.summary: September 2024 essay (prompted by a Brian Chesky talk) arguing the conventional advice - 'Hire good people and give them room to do their jobs' - fails founders at scale, while conceding 'Obviously founders can't keep running a 2000 person company the way they ran it when it had 20.'
artifacts.lesson: Delegation norms that work for professional managers can hollow out founder-led companies.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Player crosses into City stage (1,000+) and chooses to keep direct control over research priorities.

artifacts.title: The only thing that matters
artifacts.quote: The only thing that matters is getting to product/market fit.
artifacts.speaker: Marc Andreessen
artifacts.summary: pmarchive 'Guide to Startups part 4'. Defines PMF as 'being in a good market with a product that can satisfy that market'. Credits Andy Rachleff (ex-Benchmark) with 'Rachleff's Law of Startup Success': 'The #1 company-killer is lack of market.' Also: 'In a great market—a market with lots of real potential customers—the market pulls product out of the startup.'
artifacts.lesson: Market beats team and product; a great market pulls the product out of you.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Demand exceeds compute/serving capacity for the first time ('customers buying as fast as you can make it').

artifacts.title: An engine to find product/market fit
artifacts.quote: Within just three quarters of our work to improve the product, the score nearly doubled to 58%.
artifacts.speaker: Rahul Vohra (First Round Review)
artifacts.summary: Vohra operationalized Sean Ellis's survey ('How would you feel if you could no longer use the product?'; 'Ellis found that the magic number was 40%' very disappointed). Superhuman started at 22% ('it was clear that Superhuman had not reached product-market fit') and reached 58%.
artifacts.lesson: PMF can be measured and iterated on, not just felt.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Player's 'very disappointed' survey stat crosses 40%.

artifacts.title: Find a growth hacker
artifacts.speaker: Sean Ellis
artifacts.summary: Ellis coined 'growth hacker' in his 2010 post 'Find a Growth Hacker for Your Startup', describing someone whose true north is growth; it stemmed from frustration hiring traditional marketers to replace himself. Andrew Chen popularized it in 'Growth Hacker is the new VP Marketing' (2012), using Airbnb's Craigslist integration as the case study.
artifacts.lesson: Growth became an engineering discipline, not a marketing department.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Player hires/creates a dedicated Growth team.

artifacts.title: The Craigslist integration
artifacts.quote: This kind of integration is not trivial.
artifacts.speaker: Andrew Chen
artifacts.summary: Airbnb let hosts cross-post listings to Craigslist (which had no API) via automation that filled in category/region and linked back to Airbnb, siphoning Craigslist demand. It violated Craigslist's terms on automated posting; it is cited as both a growth-hacking model and a cautionary tale. Exact year not firmly established (commonly placed ~2010-2011).
artifacts.lesson: Parasitic distribution works until the platform notices.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Player uses a gray-area distribution hack (e.g., scraping/riding a bigger platform) for users; later chance of platform retaliation.

artifacts.title: Seven friends in ten days
artifacts.speaker: Chamath Palihapitiya
artifacts.summary: Palihapitiya, who led Facebook's growth team from 2007, has described the company's 'keystone' insight as getting any new user to seven friends within 10 days, after which users rarely churned; 'People You May Know' was a key product response. Exact wording comes via secondary write-ups, no primary transcript verified. Twitter's analogue: Josh Elman's growth team found users following ~30 accounts became long-term actives (secondary sources; some accounts say 5-10 follows on day one).
artifacts.lesson: Find the activation threshold that predicts retention, then bend onboarding toward it.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Player discovers an 'activation metric' via analytics research tech.

artifacts.title: The Summer Founders Program
artifacts.speaker: Jessica Livingston
artifacts.summary: YC launched its website in March 2005 in Cambridge, MA, inviting applications to the 'Summer Founders Program' (founders: Paul Graham, Jessica Livingston, Robert Morris, Trevor Blackwell). It funded eight startups that summer at $6,000 per founder; the first batch included Reddit and Sam Altman (Loopt). Current standard deal (verified Oct 2026): $500,000 total = $125,000 on a post-money SAFE for 7% + $375,000 uncapped MFN SAFE; YC takes pro rata rights and charges no fees.
artifacts.lesson: Small cheques, batch cohorts and a Demo Day made seed investing industrial.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Player accepts an accelerator-style deal (small cash for ~7%) early in the game.

artifacts.title: From YC to OpenAI
artifacts.speaker: OpenAI ('Introducing OpenAI')
artifacts.summary: Paul Graham named Sam Altman YC president in February 2014; Altman taught Stanford CS183B 'How to Start a Startup' in fall 2014 (20 lectures, free online). OpenAI was announced in December 2015 as a nonprofit; its intro post listed Sam, Greg, Elon, Reid Hoffman, Jessica Livingston, Peter Thiel, AWS, Infosys and YC Research as donors with $1B committed. CAUTION: OpenAI was NOT a YC company or a YC Research project - YC Research (Altman's nonprofit lab, announced shortly before) was only a listed pledger, and reporting says it contributed nothing; only ~$133M of pledges had been received by 2021. Altman left the YC presidency in 2019 to focus on OpenAI; Graham (2024) disputed claims he was 'fired'.
artifacts.lesson: Accelerator networks seeded the frontier-lab era, but pledges are not cash.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Player announces a large pledged-funding round; later only a fraction arrives.

artifacts.title: The Burn Multiple
artifacts.quote: Burn Multiple = Net Burn / Net New ARR
artifacts.speaker: David Sacks
artifacts.summary: Sacks' efficiency metric: how much a startup burns for each incremental dollar of ARR. Text calls 2x 'reasonable for an early-stage startup' and 5x 'a terrible Burn Multiple'; the tier chart is in an image (see metrics).
artifacts.lesson: Growth is only impressive relative to what it costs.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Player's quarterly burn multiple exceeds 3x.

artifacts.title: Adapting to Endure
artifacts.speaker: Sequoia Capital
artifacts.summary: In May 2022 Sequoia presented a ~50-page deck ('Adapting to Endure') to ~250 portfolio founders, calling it a 'crucible moment', warning of no quick V-shaped recovery, and urging a shift from growth-at-all-costs to profitability and extended runway. Echo of its 2008 'R.I.P. Good Times' deck. Context: the end of the zero-interest-rate era as the Fed began hiking in March 2022.
artifacts.lesson: When money stops being free, 'default dead' companies are exposed all at once.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Macro event: interest rate shock raises cost of capital; valuations and new funding drop.

artifacts.title: Fast goes slow
artifacts.summary: One-click checkout startup Fast, which raised $120M+ (incl. a Stripe-led $102M round) and was seeking a $1B+ valuation, shut down abruptly in April 2022 amid high cash burn and only modest revenue.
artifacts.lesson: Growth spending without revenue is a countdown.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Burn multiple > 5 for 2+ quarters with fundraising attempt failing.

artifacts.title: Convoy's perfect storm
artifacts.speaker: Dan Lewis (memo, via Bloomberg)
artifacts.summary: Seattle freight startup Convoy, valued at $3.8B in 2022 and backed by Bezos and Gates, shut down after a four-month search for a buyer failed. CEO Dan Lewis blamed a massive freight recession and contraction in capital markets; staff had already shrunk from ~1,500 to ~500.
artifacts.lesson: A peak valuation is not a balance sheet; capital markets can close mid-sprint.
artifacts.suggested_trigger: Player fails to close a fundraise or acquisition while runway < 2 quarters.

achievements.name: Mildly Mortified
achievements.basis: Hoffman: 'If you're not embarrassed by the first version of your product, you've launched too late.'
achievements.suggested_trigger: Ship first product while its quality score is below the 'polished' threshold and still gain users.

achievements.name: Exceptionally Doing Well
achievements.basis: PG: 10% weekly growth is 'exceptionally well' (5-7% is good).

achievements.name: Instant Noodles, Infinite Leverage
achievements.suggested_trigger: Revenue covers founder/base payroll for the first time.

achievements.name: It's Alive!
achievements.suggested_trigger: Projection flips from default dead to default alive.

achievements.name: Collison Installation
achievements.basis: Stripe founders setting users up on the spot (Do Things That Don't Scale).

achievements.name: Very Disappointed (Affectionately)
achievements.basis: Sean Ellis 40% 'very disappointed' PMF test; Superhuman 22% -> 58%.

achievements.name: This Is Fine
achievements.suggested_trigger: Survive a quarter with 3+ unresolved incidents and still hit growth target.

achievements.name: Triple Triple Double Double Double
achievements.suggested_trigger: Annual revenue 3x, 3x, 2x, 2x, 2x over five consecutive years.

achievements.name: Some Assembly Required
achievements.basis: Hoffman's 'jumping off a cliff and assembling the airplane on the way down' (image originally Bradbury's).
achievements.suggested_trigger: Reach break-even with < 1 month of runway left.

metrics.name: Weekly growth rate (PG)
metrics.definition: Week-over-week growth in the key metric (revenue, or active users if pre-revenue).

metrics.name: Burn Multiple
metrics.definition: Net Burn / Net New ARR (per period).

thresholds.note: Tier chart is an image in Sacks' post and widely reproduced; the post text itself confirms 2x 'reasonable for an early-stage startup' and 5x 'terrible'.

metrics.name: Sean Ellis PMF test
metrics.definition: % of active users answering 'very disappointed' to 'How would you feel if you could no longer use [product]?' (exclude 'no longer use' respondents).

metrics.name: T2D3
metrics.definition: From ~$1-2M ARR: triple, triple, double, double, double annually (e.g. $2M -> 6 -> 18 -> 36 -> 72 -> 144M) to reach $100M+ ARR in ~5-6 years.
metrics.source: https://battery.com/blog/a-mantra-for-saas-success-triple-triple-double-double-double (Neeraj Agrawal, Battery Ventures; first published on TechCrunch as 'The SaaS Adventure', 2015)

metrics.name: Rule of 40
metrics.definition: Revenue growth rate (%) + profit margin (%, Feld used EBITDA as baseline) >= 40.
metrics.source: Brad Feld, 'The Rule of 40% For a Healthy SaaS Company' (Feb 2015); summarized at https://www.holistics.io/blog/intuition-of-the-rule-of-40/

metrics.name: Default alive / dead
metrics.definition: Holding expenses constant and extrapolating recent revenue growth, does the company reach profitability before cash runs out?
